The NVRAM technology has become a widely adopted storage medium in high-performance computing systems, offering substantial capacity and speed enhancements. NVRAM accelerators can be integrated into various applications, including machine learning, data analytics, and scientific computing, to boost performance and efficiency. However, the integration of NVRAM accelerators poses significant challenges, particularly in terms of software development and system integration. To address these challenges, we introduce NVAcc, a software framework that streamlines the integration of NVRAM accelerators into existing applications. NVAcc is designed to be compatible with a wide range of NVRAM devices and provides a unified interface for developers to leverage the capabilities of different accelerators. Our evaluation of NVAcc with four NVRAM devices and three applications demonstrates its effectiveness in achieving performance gains of up to 10.5 times over the baseline, with a speedup of up to 10 times for a particular application.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have demonstrated its potential in enhancing classification performance, particularly in scenarios with limited training data. This study investigates the efficacy of contrastive self-supervised learning in conjunction with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) classification, a field plagued by a scarcity of medical data. We introduce a novel approach that integrates contrastive self-supervised learning with convolutional neural networks, a technique that has shown promise in enhancing classification performance. We evaluate the effectiveness of this method on fMRI classification tasks, specifically Alzheimer's disease and autism spectrum disorder classification, and demonstrate its superiority over conventional methods in terms of classification accuracy.

We demonstrate that two real-valued, non-degenerate bilinear forms on a vector space can be transformed into each other using a specific type of operation if and only if they share the same valuated normal form. This relationship holds true for the specific case of a bilinear form derived from a vector space's induced structure. Furthermore, we show that the valuated normal form of these forms remains constant under the valuated field's group of transformations. Our findings also reveal that the remaining ambiguity in the valuated normal form's value lies in its signature modulo 8.

Researchers have recently made a breakthrough in observing the emission of high-energy photons from the interaction of electrons with the light emitted by accelerated electrons in a laser-irradiated beryllium target. This observation was made possible by the use of a laser with a high power density, which caused the accelerated electrons to emit X-rays. The emitted X-rays were then converted into high-energy photons by the interaction with the laser, which in turn produced Cherenkov radiation in the beryllium target. The results of this observation are significant, as they provide a promising method for generating high-energy gamma-ray beams using laser-irradiated targets.

This involves recognizing arguments within a text that are not explicitly expressed but can be inferred from context. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the existing literature on this subject, including a detailed examination of the types of implicit arguments, datasets used, evaluation methods, and current approaches. The study also explores the various types of implicit arguments, including those related to causality, possession, time, and space. The diagnosis of medical images is a complex task that requires the integration of multiple features.  Although deep learning models have been widely used for automated disease diagnosis, they often fail to provide accurate results due to the lack of interpretability.  Most traditional loss functions used in these models are based on the assumption that the model can learn the entire feature space, which is not always the case.  This paper proposes a novel loss function that incorporates the concept of "all or nothing" to improve the model's ability to learn the most important features.  By doing so, the model can focus on the most relevant features and avoid learning irrelevant ones.  This new loss function is tested on a large dataset of chest X-ray images and shows significant improvements in terms of accuracy and robustness.

In a Bayesian framework, we develop an approach to identify the most effective model from a set of available models, using the Akaike information criterion. This method is grounded in the concept of predictive probability and provides a clear connection to the traditional AIC. We also establish a threshold for the predictive probability, which can be set based on the number of models under consideration. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a simulation study and compare it to traditional methods, including a Monte Carlo method and a Dirichlet distribution. Additionally, we showcase the practical application of this method in a real-world scenario involving the analysis of COVID-19 data.

Our research focuses on the binary patterns found within the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence, denoted as $(\pi_n)_{n \ge 0}$. We have established that any non-empty binary string can be found within this sequence, except for a few specific patterns. These exceptions include a single '1', a string consisting of $n$ ones for $n \ge 2$, and specific patterns with a single '1' surrounded by varying numbers of zeros. We have also proven that certain patterns with a single '1' and varying numbers of zeros on either side are present within this sequence. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence contains all patterns with a single run of zeros and all patterns with two runs of zeros. We have also shown that the sequence contains all patterns with a single run of ones and all patterns with two runs of ones.

A new method for dynamic classifier selection has been developed, which dynamically identifies the most suitable classifier for specific test instances. This technique is applied to the test set, allowing each instance to be classified by the most effective classifier. A technique known as the "select" method is proposed, which involves training a classifier to determine the most suitable one for each test instance. This method is then compared to other techniques, such as stacking, to determine its effectiveness. This technique is further applied to the domain of multi-label learning, which involves classifying multiple labels for each instance. A multi-label classifier is trained to select the most suitable classifier for each instance, which is then used to classify the instance. This technique is evaluated using a benchmark dataset and found to outperform other methods in multi-label learning.

Our study establishes and utilizes an interpolation theorem to derive a condition for strict positive definiteness in metric spaces. This condition is both necessary and sufficient, and we leverage it to explore the implications for metric embeddings. Additionally, we explore the connection between strict positive definiteness and injectivity in metric spaces, as well as the equivalence of two definitions for injectivity.

The attributable fraction among the exposed (EF) represents the proportion of disease cases in a population that could be avoided if a specific exposure were eliminated. EF is a crucial metric for assessing the impact of public health interventions. Despite its importance, researchers have yet to develop an EF estimator that is statistically robust and reliable. In this study, we introduce a novel method for estimating EF using a double machine learning approach, which allows for more accurate predictions of disease outcomes and exposure effects. Our proposed method is evaluated through simulations and applied to a real-world example to demonstrate its effectiveness.

We extend Kato-Saito's $K$-theoretic $g$-complex to schemes with singularities and derive Bloch's formula for their Chow groups of 0-cycles. This results in the computation of the Chow groups of 0-cycles for certain singular curves and surfaces with $G_m$-schemes action.

The production of excited mesons, including D* and f2*, relative to their ground states, D and phi, has been studied in relation to the number of particles produced in pp collisions at a 5.02 TeV energy. The results show that the ratios of cross-sections for D0 to D*0 and phi to f2*(2H12) vary significantly with particle multiplicity, while the ratios for D+ to D*(1285) and D*(2007) and phi to f2*(2H12) remain relatively constant. These findings suggest that the production of excited mesons is influenced by the number of particles produced in the collision.

We investigate the spin entropy in a double quantum dot system, specifically focusing on the Kondo effect. The system is characterized by a double quantum dot coupled to a ferromagnetic lead, where the first layer exhibits Kondo correlations and the second layer is a spin-1/2 coupled to a bath, also displaying Kondo correlations. By employing the numerical renormalization group method, we analyze the spin entropy in the Kondo regime, where the spin entropy of the spin-1/2 is equivalent to that of the first layer. The study reveals that the spin entropy is influenced by the interlayer coupling, leading to a spin entropy that is less than the sum of the individual layer spin entropies. The findings are validated by comparing them with the numerical results.

Consider a polynomial P(z) of degree n and a zero of P(z) at z0. In the vicinity of z0, the modulus of P(z) resembles |z-z0|^k, where k is the multiplicity of z0. This k divides n and creates n/k equal sectors at z0, with angles π/k, where P(z) alternates between increasing and decreasing in magnitude. We establish that the boundary between these increasing and decreasing regions is comprised of curves along which P(z) remains constant in argument. We also prove two theorems regarding the behavior of these sectors and curves. The first theorem demonstrates that sectors and curves are always either smooth or have a specific type of singularity at z0. The second theorem shows that, except for specific cases, the boundary between these increasing and decreasing regions is a smooth curve with a singular point at z0.

We investigate the stability of bright solitons in a Bose-Einstein condensate, taking into account the effects of a transverse magnetic field and attractive dipole-dipole interactions. By employing the variational method, we derive the soliton's width and amplitude, and our findings are validated through numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that the solitons' stability is influenced by the interplay between the magnetic field and dipole-dipole interactions. Furthermore, we find that the solitons' width and amplitude exhibit distinct behaviors depending on the magnetic field's direction. Our study provides valuable insights into the stability of bright solitons in the presence of both magnetic fields and long-range interactions.

This study focuses on approximating the geometric-arithmetic mean inequality through a series of linear constraints, thereby enabling the transformation of complex optimization problems into linear programs. A sequence of pre-defined inequalities is developed to provide a precise and efficient approximation of the geometric-arithmetic mean inequality. The proposed method is demonstrated to yield a tight approximation, and its effectiveness is showcased through numerical experiments.

The Teichmüller space Teichm(M) of a manifold M can be represented as a union of Teichmüller orbit spaces, each orbit being the Teichmüller space Teichm/M^i, where M^i represents the Teichmüller equivalence classes in Mod^i, the Teichmüller equivalence classes of the mapping class group Mod^1.

We introduce a groundbreaking method for generating photorealistic virtual avatars from a single, low-resolution RGB-D video sequence. Our approach leverages the unique characteristics of RGB-D sequences to accurately capture the avatar's individualized shape and texture. By incorporating a shape prior, we ensure that the avatar's geometry is both realistic and consistent. Furthermore, we utilize a texture prior to ensure that the avatar's appearance is both detailed and coherent. By combining these priors with a deep learning-based optimization framework, we can produce high-quality, personalized avatars from a single video sequence. Our method outperforms existing techniques in terms of realism and accuracy, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through a range of experiments and applications.

Reconstructing a 3D face model from images is a challenging task due to the occurrence of occlusions. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach that utilizes a combination of a generative adversarial network and a deep learning-based method. Our proposed method, called 3DGAN, incorporates a 3D-aware loss function to ensure the generated mesh aligns with the input image. To overcome the limitations of traditional loss functions, we employ a 2D-to-3D correspondence method that matches image pixels with 3D points on the mesh. Furthermore, we incorporate a 2D-to-3D loss function to improve the accuracy of the generated mesh. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

In a reinforcement learning framework, we're investigating the balance between exploration and exploitation, where an agent must decide whether to stick with a known, high-reward action or try a less familiar one that could potentially yield a higher reward. To address this challenge, we've developed a novel approach that combines the success of multi-armed bandit algorithms with the need for efficient exploration in reinforcement learning. By applying the Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) method, we've adapted it to handle the complexities of reinforcement learning, where the reward is uncertain and the environment is dynamic. Our method is grounded in the idea that the value of an action can be estimated using its upper confidence bound, which is calculated based on the number of times the action has been taken. By incorporating this UCB value into the Q-learning process, we've been able to improve the agent's ability to explore the environment efficiently and make informed decisions. Our results demonstrate that this UCB-Q method outperforms traditional Q-learning in a variety of scenarios, particularly when the environment is complex and the agent has limited exploration time.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, the complexity of the joint action space poses a significant challenge to policy optimization. A novel localized approach to deep reinforcement learning is proposed to tackle this issue. By focusing on the joint action space around the current action, the method aims to find the optimal policy more efficiently. A novel algorithm, Localized Double Q-Network (LDQN), is developed to achieve this goal. LDQN employs a local exploration strategy to select the next action, and a two-network architecture to estimate Q-values. By combining local exploration with a two-network approach, LDQN can effectively learn the optimal policy in complex environments. Experimental results demonstrate LDQN's superiority over existing algorithms in various domains, including Atari games, grid worlds, and multi-agent scenarios.

This research investigates the thermoelectric properties of penta-silicene, a two-dimensional material, using the Boltzmann transport equation and the relaxation time approximation. The study reveals that penta-silicene exhibits exceptional thermoelectric performance at room temperature, primarily due to its low effective mass and high carrier mobility. The material's low out-of-plane thermal conductivity and high in-plane thermal conductivity also contribute to its high thermoelectric efficiency. The results show that penta-silicene has a high thermoelectric figure of merit, with values of 2.4 for holes and 2.1 for electrons at room temperature. The study also explores the effects of strain on the thermoelectric properties of penta-silicene, revealing that the material's thermoelectric efficiency can be significantly enhanced under certain conditions. The results of this study have important implications for the development of high-performance thermoelectric devices based on penta-silicene.

In a study, we examined how hot magnetized environments affect the binding of quarks and gluons, a type of subatomic particle. We used a mathematical model to understand how quarks and gluons interact in such conditions, and we applied this model to predict how quarks and gluons bind in a hot magnetized environment. We focused on two types of bound states, charmonium and bottomonium, and calculated how quarks and gluons bind in such conditions, taking into account the effects of heat and magnetism. We found that the effects of heat and magnetism on quark binding are significant and can lead to changes in the binding energy of quarks and gluons. We also found that the binding energy of quarks and gluons is sensitive to changes in the temperature and magnetic field strength, and that the binding energy of quarks and gluons can be used to understand the properties of hot magnetized environments.

The interaction between dark matter and Standard Model particles can be detected through observations of astrophysical and cosmological phenomena. This research examines the potential of using fast radio bursts to detect dark matter annihilations. Annihilations of dark matter particles within the galactic halo could produce photons that are observed as fast radio bursts. We investigate the sensitivity of these bursts to detect dark matter annihilations and compare them with other detection methods. We also explore the potential of using fast radio bursts to detect dark matter in the early universe.

Green Security Problems have proven effective in formulating optimal patrol strategies to safeguard valuable resources. However, existing solutions are often limited by their reliance on linear programming, which restricts the complexity of the models they can handle. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel Green Security Problem model that incorporates resource dynamics, allowing for a more realistic representation of resource interactions. Our model is solved using a combination of reinforcement learning and linear programming. The resulting algorithm demonstrates the feasibility of our approach by successfully applying it to a complex scenario involving a large number of resources and patrol units.

This paper proposes a robot navigation system that effectively tackles the challenges posed by uneven terrain. To achieve this, we've developed a novel attention mask that integrates key features such as terrain height, slope, and elevation changes. These features are derived from a depth map generated by a depth sensor. Our system is built upon a fully-convolutional neural network, which is trained using a dataset of labeled depth maps. To evaluate its performance, we've created a dataset of depth maps from various real-world scenarios, including both flat and uneven terrains. Our system is then tested in a simulated environment, where it demonstrates the ability to navigate challenging terrains, including those with obstacles.

The interplay between disorder and frustration in magnetic materials is a complex phenomenon, particularly when considering the impact of uniaxial anisotropy. We have developed a theoretical framework to investigate how this factor influences disorder and frustration in a two-dimensional Ising model with random interactions. Our analysis reveals that the introduction of uniaxial anisotropy leads to a reduction in disorder and frustration, with the former two exhibiting a linear relationship in the presence of a magnetic field. We have also identified a critical threshold for anisotropy strength, beyond which the spin-glass phase is completely eliminated. Our findings have potential applications in understanding the behavior of magnetic materials with random properties.

This study develops a comprehensive theory for the generalized polarization tensors in two-dimensional planar conductivity inclusions, encompassing both standard and edge polarization tensors. A key aspect of this theory is the utilization of the Cauchy integral operator on two-dimensional domains with multiple boundaries. The developed framework enables the derivation of explicit formulas for the GPTs and provides a method for their computation. The edge polarization tensor presents a unique challenge due to the logarithmic singularity of the GPT matrix, which is resolved through a novel approach. The proposed framework is further validated through numerical examples demonstrating the accuracy of the developed formulas.

The development of magnetic instabilities within stars is investigated using a comprehensive model that accounts for the dynamic interaction between magnetic fields and fluid flow. This model, which is based on the principles of magnetohydrodynamics, allows for the examination of magnetic field configurations in a spherical environment. It has been demonstrated that a specific type of magnetic field configuration, which is characterized by a radial symmetry, is inherently unstable and can lead to the emergence of new magnetic structures. Furthermore, the instability of these magnetic structures is found to be influenced by the properties of the fluid flow and the strength of the magnetic field.

We propose a novel concept of synchronization for a specific class of networks that operate on simplicial complexes. This class of networks is characterized by a specific type of interaction, allowing for the synchronization of vertices that are connected by a shared link. We establish that two such networks will synchronize if and only if there is a direct connection between the vertices that are connected by a link, and this connection is facilitated by a shared link. This finding provides insight into the conditions necessary for the synchronization of networks that operate on simplicial complexes.

Sparse matrix-vector multiplication and linear solvers are crucial components of scientific research and engineering, and they are frequently used in large-scale computations.  The efficiency of these algorithms heavily relies on the performance of sparse matrix-vector multiplication and linear solver operations.  To address this need, the VNNI sparsity extension for sparse matrix-vector multiplication and linear solver operations has been developed.  The extension incorporates a new memory access instruction that allows for efficient memory access and reduces memory access overhead.  The extension also introduces a new instruction format that enables the efficient processing of sparse matrix-vector multiplication and linear solver operations.  The VNNI sparsity extension has been integrated into the AMDGPU architecture, and experimental results demonstrate that it significantly improves the performance of sparse matrix-vector multiplication and linear solver operations.  The extension has been shown to achieve a speedup of up to 2.5 times compared to the baseline, and it has been found to be effective for a wide range of sparse matrix-vector multiplication and linear solver operations.

We establish a theorem in the complex plane that generalizes the concept of sharing points partially, effectively solving a long-standing conjecture by Paulsen. Specifically, for a normal family G of meromorphic functions on a domain D, where all limit functions are non-constant, any other family of meromorphic functions F that shares a specific point with G, consisting of at least three distinct elements, must itself be normal in D, thereby also yielding a result concerning the uniqueness of such functions.

Human teams collaborate by sharing intentions, but their interactions are not always fully transparent. This study examines how humans share intentions in a collaborative context, utilizing a game where a team member must identify a hidden sequence of targets. The research reveals that while humans often share their intentions, they do not disclose all of their plans, and instead, they tend to share their primary objectives and the steps required to achieve them. The findings suggest that a model of intention sharing can be developed, which can be applied to improve human-robot teams by enabling robots to better understand and respond to human needs.

This research focuses on the algebraic properties of non-integrable bi-decomposable Monge-Ampere systems, particularly those of rank 3, 2, and 1, which are characterized by Lagrangian pairs. The study reveals a unique method for classifying non-integrable bi-decomposable Monge-Ampere systems of rank 2, allowing for a more comprehensive understanding of their structure. The research also identifies a specific family of bi-decomposable, non-integrable Monge-Ampere systems of rank 1, which are invariant under the action of SL(2,R) x SL(2,R). The study further explores the integrability properties of bi-decomposable Monge-Ampere systems of rank 1, providing a more nuanced understanding of their structure. The research also reveals a novel method for classifying integrable bi-decomposable Monge-Ampere systems of rank 2, which are not equivalent to the Pfaffian systems associated with them. The study concludes with a more detailed classification of integrable bi-decomposable Monge-Ampere systems of rank 1, which are not equivalent to the Pfaffian systems associated with them.

The process of water electrolysis is hindered by the slow movement of gas bubbles, which form on the electrode surface and impede the flow of electricity. To better understand this issue, researchers have developed a model that simulates the growth and contraction of gas bubbles on a flat surface. The model accounts for the complex interactions between the bubbles, the electrolyte, and the electrode, which are often overlooked in previous studies. The model's results reveal that the size and spacing of the bubbles significantly influence their movement and the overall performance of the water electrolysis process. The model's findings also show that the bubbles' movement is influenced by both the electrolyte's properties and the rate at which the bubbles form. The model's predictions were validated through experiments, which revealed that the bubbles' movement is influenced by both the electrolyte's properties and the rate at which the bubbles form. The model's results also highlight the importance of optimizing the electrode's surface to improve the efficiency of the water electrolysis process.

A study has been conducted to investigate the presence of particles that live for a long time and decay into two photons, using data from the CMS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. The data, collected in 2016 and 2017, consists of 35.9 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The study focused on particles decaying outside the detector's inner region, and found no significant excess beyond the expected Standard Model background. The results were used to set limits on the lifespan of these particles, and also to search for particles predicted by a specific theory. The study found that particles with masses between 100 GeV and 1000 GeV can have lifetimes as short as 10^-9 seconds.

In the study of Dirac semimetals, we investigate the renormalization group flow of the effective action, which is derived from a microscopic model incorporating anisotropy and spin-orbit coupling. Our findings indicate that the dimensionless coupling constant and anisotropy parameters exhibit a decrease with energy reduction, ultimately leading to a flow towards a second-order Dirac semimetal phase. This flow occurs within a regime of weak fluctuations, which is characterized by a low-energy scaling theory. This theory is built upon the concept of emergent symmetries and scale invariance, which become apparent at low energies. Our analysis reveals that the scaling exponents associated with the fermion field and gauge field are equal to one-half, while the scaling exponent associated with the photon field is zero. This outcome is consistent with the predictions of the free Dirac semimetal model. Our results demonstrate that the free Dirac semimetal is an attractive fixed point in the renormalization group flow, which is reached from a broad range of initial conditions. This outcome is significant, as it suggests that the free Dirac semimetal is a universal phase that emerges from a broad range of microscopic models.

This research introduces a novel framework for reasoning with everyday knowledge to verify concurrent correctness of data structures. The framework is built on a knowledge graph that represents common sense principles governing data structures, enabling the validation of concurrent operations. The framework has been applied to a range of data structures, including lists, stacks, and binary trees, and has been implemented in the Isabelle/HOL language.

Ferromagnets suspended in a superconducting ring can be studied in a new way using the Meissner effect. By placing neodymium ferromagnets in a vertical position, they become levitated in the magnetic field generated by the current flowing through the ring. By applying an alternating current to the ring, the magnitude of the current oscillates, causing the ferromagnets to oscillate in the vertical direction. By measuring the frequency of these oscillations, the magnetic field strength of the neodymium magnets can be determined. This method can be applied to the study of superconducting materials and the investigation of their properties.

Using 36.1 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV, a measurement of the $t\bar{t}Z$ cross section in the 4ℓ channel has been conducted. The cross section was found to be 0.94 $\pm$ 0.14 (stat) $\pm$ 0.13 (syst) pb, which aligns with the predicted standard model value of 0.91 $\pm$ 0.04 pb. Additionally, a differential cross section analysis was performed, focusing on $t\bar{t}Z$ production and decay in the 4ℓ channel. The results were compared to leading order and next-to-leading order standard model predictions, and no discrepancies were observed.

We categorize the rebits under the action of $SL(2,\mathbb{R})^4$ into three groups: the generic, the real, and the imaginary orbit. A specific set of invariants is identified for rebits and the process of determining the orbit into which a rebit falls is outlined.

Predictive state representations, or PSRs, are a type of Markov representation that relies on historical sequences of actions and observations to describe a system's state. Although PSRs can be used for model-based reinforcement learning and planning, they have a significant limitation: they can't directly measure the system's reward. This paper presents a method for solving the reinforcement learning problem using PSRs, which involves converting the problem into a standard Markov decision process. By doing so, we can apply established planning techniques to the new representation. Our experiments show that this method can efficiently handle complex problems and outperform existing techniques in certain scenarios.

This study focuses on composition operators within the realm of Harmonic-Bloch type spaces, and we determine the precise criteria for such operators to be bounded, nowhere vanishing, zero-pointed, or invertible.

Electric vehicles with extended range are an emerging technology that combines the benefits of electric and conventional internal combustion engines. Research has shown that these vehicles can have a lower environmental impact than traditional cars, but their actual emissions depend on how they are used. To accurately assess the environmental impact of these vehicles, it is essential to consider the variability of their use patterns. This study uses a new approach to analyze the emissions of these vehicles by combining real-world driving data with a detailed emissions model. The results show that the environmental impact of these vehicles can vary significantly depending on their use patterns, and that their benefits are most pronounced in situations where they are used for long distances. The study also finds that the environmental impact of these vehicles can be reduced by using smaller fuel tanks, but this may come at the cost of increased emissions in situations where they are used for short distances.

The mass spectra of heavy-quark mesons are calculated using the Dyson-Schwinger and Bethe-Salpeter equations, incorporating the infrared behavior of the gluon and the quark propagator. The effects of flavor dependence in dressing functions are evaluated against available data, revealing that neglecting this dependence results in a poor mass spectrum fit.

The numerical simulation of subsurface flows often involves solving complex systems of nonlinear equations that arise from the discretization of time and space. To address this challenge, a novel approach is proposed, combining a low-rank tensor approximation with a low-dimensional manifold learning technique. This method leverages the inherent structure of the solution to significantly reduce the computational cost of solving nonlinear systems. By employing a manifold learning algorithm, the solution can be represented as a low-dimensional function, which can then be used to approximate the solution to the nonlinear system. The proposed approach is demonstrated to be effective in solving various subsurface flow applications, including the solution of nonlinear systems of equations that arise from the discretization of time and space. The results show that the proposed method can achieve significant savings in computational cost while maintaining accuracy.

Deep learning methods have been widely applied to autonomous driving behavior prediction, but their lack of interpretability poses a challenge. This work introduces a novel approach to analyze the relationship between prediction performance and driving scenarios. By examining how different deep learning models perform in various scenarios, it becomes possible to identify specific situations where predictions may be less accurate. To address this issue, a new method is proposed to analyze the correlation between prediction accuracy and driving scenarios. This method involves using a deep learning model to analyze the prediction results and generate a new dataset that can be used to improve the prediction accuracy. By applying this method, it becomes possible to identify specific situations where prediction accuracy is low and develop targeted strategies to improve prediction accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in improving prediction accuracy and reducing the occurrence of low prediction accuracy scenarios.

The GaN MESFET is a potential candidate for solid-state electronics in the near future. Our research focuses on the performance of GaN MESFET devices at low temperatures, specifically at 4 Kelvin. Our experiments show that these devices exhibit a temperature-dependent decrease in current, which is caused by the presence of trap centers in the GaN material. To mitigate this issue, we employed a two-dimensional simulation to analyze the impact of different trap center concentrations on the device's performance. Our findings indicate that the presence of trap centers significantly affects the device's performance, especially at low temperatures, leading to a substantial increase in the number of trap centers required to achieve a noticeable increase in the device's current.

This study introduces a novel approach to identifying and eliminating false GNSS signals within a tracking loop, which can be integrated into existing software-defined GNSS receivers. Urban environments pose significant challenges to traditional tracking loops, leading to the development of this innovative solution. The proposed tracker employs advanced statistical methods to identify and discard false GNSS signals, leveraging the temporal and spatial relationships between them. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding improved positioning accuracy and reduced processing times.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach for analyzing complex high-dimensional tensor data, which is particularly useful in fields like neuroimaging and genetics. The proposed method, known as the tensor-variate factor analysis model, is an extension of the factor analysis model that incorporates a specific prior distribution. The model's parameters are estimated using a combination of Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, including Gibbs sampling and collapsed Gibbs sampling. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to accurately recover data patterns and perform variable selection in a simulated study, as well as in a real-world application involving the analysis of gene expression data from a neurodegenerative disease.

This research presents a novel approach to visually tracking a fast-moving object by integrating an event camera into the vision system. Traditional cameras often struggle to accurately track rapidly moving objects due to their limited temporal resolution, resulting in streak artifacts. To address this limitation, we utilize an event camera, which captures changes in brightness at high temporal resolutions. To further enhance the tracking performance, we combine the event camera with a conventional camera, leveraging the strengths of both sensors. The proposed method involves a two-stage process: first, an event camera-based tracker predicts the object's motion, and then a conventional camera-based tracker refines this prediction. The performance of our approach is evaluated on the high-speed dataset, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in tracking rapidly moving objects.

A multi-level cache-enabled network is an innovative approach that allows for improved network efficiency by incorporating cache capabilities at the edge nodes. In this type of network, a substantial portion of data traffic is redirected to the edge cache, minimizing the need for backhaul and base station transmissions. However, the limited capacity of the cache poses a significant challenge. In response, a novel framework for cache-enabled networks is proposed, which integrates a hierarchical caching system with a graph-based association strategy. The proposed framework, specifically designed for multi-level cache networks, utilizes a hierarchical caching system to store frequently accessed content and a graph-based association strategy to optimize user connectivity. The proposed framework is evaluated through simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in reducing network latency and improving overall network efficiency.

A conjecture proposed by J. Kraus in 1973, known as Kraus's conjecture, states that the positive partial transpose of no more than $\dim(\mathcal{H})-1$ Hermitian matrices of full rank in a finite-dimensional space $\mathcal{H}$ must yield a positive operator. This conjecture has been confirmed for specific cases, but a more recent and relevant problem concerns proving the Positive Partial Transpose (PPT) square for a finite number of matrices. We have developed a proof for the PPT square in a finite-dimensional space $\mathcal{H}$, given that a set of $\mathcal{H}$'s Hermitian matrices $\{H_i\}_{i=1}^n$ has a positive partial transpose and the number of matrices $n$ is less than or equal to $\dim(\mathcal{H})-1$. This result confirms Kraus's conjecture. Furthermore, we have shown that the positive partial transpose of Hermitian matrices $H_1, \ldots, H_n$ in a finite-dimensional space $\mathcal{H}$, with $n$ being less than or equal to $\dim(\mathcal{H})-1$, implies that these matrices are simultaneously diagonalizable.

A Cayley graph is considered normal edge-transitive if its full automorphism group preserves its edge-transitivity. This study identifies the structure of normal edge-transitive Cayley graphs, revealing that a Cayley graph is normal edge-transitive if and only if its corresponding automorphism group includes a specific normal subgroup that is invariant under the graph's automorphism group.

This paper tackles the challenge of optimizing sensor placement for a mobile robot's localization, using a novel approach that incorporates the robot's trajectory and a trajectory planner. To address the limitations of existing methods, which often rely on fixed sensor positions or fixed robot paths, we introduce a multi-stage optimization process that iteratively refines sensor placement and robot path. Our method involves a two-step process: first, we optimize the sensor positions to minimize the worst-case Dilution of Precision, and then we incorporate the robot's trajectory into the optimization. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields more effective sensor placement compared to existing methods.

A widely recognized formula, the Debye model, describes the relationship between shear modulus and shear wave velocity in condensed matter systems. However, recent studies have found that this formula does not accurately describe the shear wave dispersion in monolayer graphene. This paper presents a revised formula, the modified Debye model, which incorporates the effects of both linear and quadratic dispersion relations. By applying the modified Debye model, we demonstrate that the shear wave dispersion in monolayer graphene can be accurately described, and that the formula provides a more precise fit than the traditional Debye model.

Deep learning-based motion deblurring techniques have garnered significant attention in the field, yet their performance is often hindered by the lack of high-quality paired training data. Consequently, synthetic blur data is frequently employed, yet this approach fails to accurately replicate real-world blur characteristics. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel data synthesis method that leverages a deblurring model to generate realistic data. By utilizing a pre-trained deblurring model, we can produce a range of blurred images with corresponding sharp images, thereby creating a more realistic training dataset. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method, which yields a deblurring model capable of producing results comparable to those of a model trained on paired data.

The occurrence of tidal disruption events in the nearby universe is estimated to be around 10 per year, making them relatively rare. Consequently, only a few dozen TDEs have been identified to date. This scarcity hinders our understanding of supermassive black holes' spin characteristics, which are crucial for the development of theories explaining the formation and evolution of galaxies. This study presents a novel method for determining the spin of supermassive black holes by analyzing the optical light curves of TDEs. By simulating TDEs with varying spin values and analyzing their optical light curves, we discovered that the spin of a black hole can be inferred from the time it takes for the light to decrease by half. This method was successfully applied to 10 TDEs, revealing that 7 of them likely have black holes with spin values exceeding 0.5. This finding suggests that TDEs can be used to identify a substantial number of supermassive black holes with high spin values in the nearby universe.

We investigated the effect of the local environment on the Ly$\alpha$ transmission at $z\sim$6 using data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Keck telescope. Recent photometric surveys of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) have revealed a distinct color pattern, with cold classicals exhibiting bluer hues than the scattered disk and the main belt. A study of 16 newly discovered TNOs in the cold classical region found that they are notably bluer than expected, with color measurements ranging from 0.1 to 1.1. This bluer coloration is consistent with the trend observed in other surveys, suggesting a common origin for these objects. A comparison of the color distribution of the newly discovered TNOs with the main belt and scattered disk objects indicates that the latter two groups have redder colors, with cold classicals showing the most significant difference. A possible explanation for this color pattern is the presence of a common parent body for the bluest TNOs, which could have been disrupted by a collision, leading to the formation of the current population. This theory is supported by the fact that the newly discovered TNOs are among the bluest known in the outer solar system.

A novel computational model has been developed to predict the mechanical properties of Ti-6Al alloys at temperatures ranging from 200 to 600 K. This model, based on a combination of crystal plasticity and dislocation dynamics, accounts for the interactions between dislocations and various microstructural features, including grain boundaries and second-phase particles. It incorporates the effects of dislocation interactions with these features, as well as the influence of temperature on dislocation mobility. The model's predictions for yield strength and work hardening rates were compared to experimental data, showing good agreement. The model's predictions for the evolution of dislocation density and subgrain size also demonstrated reasonable accuracy. The model's ability to predict mechanical properties at different temperatures and strain rates makes it a valuable tool for designing and optimizing Ti-6Al alloys for various applications.

Software product lines consist of related products that share a commonality, and their variability is often described using feature models.  These models define a feature hierarchy and relationships between features, allowing for the creation of product configurations.  However, the complexity of feature models can make it difficult to comprehend their structure and relationships.  To address this issue, we propose a novel visualization method that highlights the structural aspects of feature models.  Our approach is evaluated through a controlled study involving feature models of varying complexity, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in conveying structural information.

High contrast imaging techniques have enabled the detection of numerous distant companions to nearby stars, but the scarcity of these companions in the inner regions remains a challenge. To overcome this, we have developed a new method that utilizes the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 to search for faint companions in the vicinity of nearby stars. By applying this method to a sample of 100 stars, we have identified 11 new companions, including a potential binary system consisting of a brown dwarf and a main-sequence star. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in detecting faint companions at small separations, and we have also estimated the completeness rate of this method to be 80% for companions with a contrast of 10 magnitudes and a separation of 0.5 arcseconds. Furthermore, we have used our data to constrain the frequency of binary systems in the vicinity of nearby stars, and we have found that the frequency of binary systems with a brown dwarf companion is lower than previously estimated. Our results have also provided new insights into the properties of these companions, including their masses and ages.

We examine the evolution of black hole evaporation in charged AdS$_4$ space, employing the Page curve framework. Our investigation focuses on symmetry-resolved entropies, which are relevant to the information paradox in quantum gravity. We derive a symmetry-resolved replica wormhole solution for a theory with a specific higher-derivative interaction and a charged scalar field. Our analysis reveals that the generalized extremal surface's symmetry-resolved entanglement entropy can be calculated using the functional renormalization group method. We find that a specific higher-derivative interaction leads to a monotonic increase in the entropy of shared symmetry-resolved states.

We have developed a novel approach to examine the Fermi surface of Weyl semimetals, focusing on the Fermi arcs that emerge. By employing a novel mathematical formalism, we've been able to identify and analyze the topology of these arcs, which is crucial for understanding their behavior. Our findings suggest that the Fermi arcs' structure is highly dependent on the orientation of the crystal, and we've developed a method to determine the Fermi arcs' shape and size in response to different crystal axes. Our research has significant implications for the study of topological semimetals, and may provide new insights into the complex interplay between topology and Fermi surface structure.

We introduce a novel video prediction approach that trains a single model to
generate predictions for any desired duration. Our method relies on an extended
sequence of frames, which enables the model to learn both short-term and
long-term dynamics simultaneously. To achieve this, we employ a unique training
strategy that utilizes a mix of short and long prediction intervals. Our method
yields a single model that can generate accurate predictions for any time frame,
unlike previous approaches requiring separate models for each duration. Our
results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving state-of-the-
art performance on the KITTI dataset, while also providing competitive results
on the ETH/Scenes dataset.

Mutations in mitochondrial DNA are closely linked to aging and cell death, but surprisingly, some research suggests that certain mtDNA mutations might actually be beneficial for healthy aging. This study focuses on the role of mitochondrial DNA in healthy aging by examining the dynamics of DNA mutations within the context of a unique cellular environment. By using a novel approach, we have developed a comprehensive model that accounts for the complex interactions between different types of DNA mutations. This model allows us to analyze the behavior of DNA mutations in both healthy and diseased cells, revealing a distinct pattern of mutation dynamics that is distinct from nuclear DNA. By examining the effects of various factors, such as cell division and environmental stress, we have gained new insights into the role of mitochondrial DNA in healthy aging. Our findings suggest that mitochondrial DNA mutations may play a more significant role in healthy aging than previously thought, and that understanding the dynamics of DNA mutations within the context of a unique cellular environment is essential for developing effective strategies for healthy aging.

This study introduces a straightforward method for mel-spectrogram generation in non-autoregressive speech synthesis, which is applicable to both discrete and continuous input data. The proposed approach is based on the observation that mel-spectrograms can be approximated by sinusoidal patterns. By utilizing a sinusoidal embedding layer, the model can learn mel-spectrograms from the embedded data. The model's performance is evaluated using the FastSpeech2 framework, demonstrating that the proposed method can achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art methods, while also showing its potential for use with continuous input data.

The amorphous and crystalline phases of Ge-Sb-Te alloys display contrasting electronic properties, making them suitable for use in optical storage and non-volatile memory. To investigate the electronic properties of these phases, we employed a combination of experimental and computational methods. Our results indicate that the optical conductivity of the amorphous phase is significantly higher than that of the crystalline phase, primarily due to the presence of a large number of localized states in the amorphous phase. This finding is consistent with our computational model, which suggests that the amorphous phase is characterized by a large density of localized states near the band edge. Our results also reveal that the optical conductivity of the amorphous phase is highly sensitive to the composition of the alloy, with the addition of Sb leading to a significant increase in the optical conductivity. This finding is consistent with our computational model, which suggests that the addition of Sb leads to a significant increase in the density of localized states. Overall, our results provide new insights into the electronic properties of Ge-Sb-Te alloys, and highlight the importance of considering both the amorphous and crystalline phases when designing materials for optical storage and non-volatile memory applications.

We then investigate the effects of symmetry breaking on this phase, revealing the presence of new phases such as the fractional topological insulator and the fractional topological insulator. We investigate the impact of a midplane gap in a protoplanetary disc on its thermal structure and radiation. Our research focuses on a simplified model of a flat, flat accretion disc with a single gap, where the disc's surface is heated by the energy released from the accretion process. We use a 1D model to study the disc's thermal structure and radiation, where the disc's surface is divided into two zones: a gap-adjacent zone and a distant zone. Our results show that the temperature of the midplane region is significantly lower than in a solid disc, particularly in the distant zone. This is because the gap reduces the disc's optical depth, allowing more radiation to escape. We also find that the disc's temperature is highly dependent on the accretion rate and the size of the gap. Our findings suggest that the midplane gap may play a significant role in the formation of planets and the evolution of protoplanetary discs.

In this study, we explore the effectiveness of data augmentation in enhancing reinforcement learning performance, particularly in scenarios involving complex observations. A novel technique, called Augmented Reinforcement Learning (AugRL), is introduced, which integrates data augmentation into the reinforcement learning process. The proposed method involves applying data augmentation to observations during the training phase, thereby increasing the diversity of the training data and improving the generalization capability of the reinforcement learning agent. The efficacy of AugRL is evaluated in a range of environments, including Atari games, locomotion tasks, and robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to significantly improve the performance of reinforcement learning agents in these scenarios. Furthermore, the impact of various augmentation techniques on the performance of AugRL is investigated, and the results indicate that certain augmentation techniques are more effective than others in different environments. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the role of data augmentation in reinforcement learning and provide a foundation for future research in this area.

A vast majority of the world's population, estimated at 300-400 million, speaks Arabic natively.  Despite this, Arabic remains a major challenge for NLP systems, due to the complexity of its dialects and the scarcity of high-quality data.  To address this, we introduce a novel approach for generating realistic Arabic dialect data using a combination of a multilingual language model and a contrastive learning technique.  This method allows us to create a large dataset of 1.5 million sentences in 10 different Arabic dialects, which we then use to train a transformer-based model capable of accurately recognizing the dialect of a given sentence.  Our model achieves a remarkable accuracy of 80.5% on a challenging benchmark dataset, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin.

We have developed a method to estimate the mass of galaxy clusters from Compton-y maps, using a Gaussian process to model the Compton-y signal. This approach is grounded in the assumption that the Compton-y signal is directly related to the cluster's gravitational potential. We have applied this method to the Planck satellite's Compton-y maps and compared the results with X-ray and Sunyaev-Zeldovich data. The mass estimates from the Compton-y data are consistent with those from the other datasets, with a slight tendency to be lower. We have also used the method to estimate the relationship between a cluster's X-ray luminosity and its mass, finding a slope of 1.19. This relationship is in line with the predictions of the Lambda Cold Dark Matter model.

The Topic2Vec approach is a novel topic modeling method designed for languages
without clear word boundaries. It utilizes a Pearson's chi-squared test or t-statistic
to identify significant correlations between adjacent characters, resulting in tokens
that are then used to train a word2vec model. The created model's topics are
derived from the clusters of model vectors. The proposed method is evaluated on
Indonesian and Vietnamese news datasets, yielding superior topic quality compared
to other approaches.

The growing number of pulsar candidates in the ASKAP EMU survey has led to an increase in the number of false positives, which is hindering the effectiveness of the follow-up observations. Aiming to improve the accuracy of the classification, we employed a machine learning approach using the XGBoost algorithm to identify pulsar candidates in the ASKAP EMU survey. By incorporating a novel method to handle the class imbalance issue, we were able to achieve a high recall rate of 85% and a high precision of 90% in our model. Our results show that the proposed method is effective in addressing the class imbalance issue and can be applied to other datasets with similar problems.

In this paper, we investigate the relationship between the context of Fell bundles over discrete groups and the subalgebra formed by the Fell bundles' Fourier subalgebra. Specifically, we demonstrate that the amenability of the underlying group is equivalent to the existence of a bounded approximate identity within the Fell bundles' Fourier subalgebra. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an inverse bimodule map for the Fell bundles' Fourier transform, thereby providing a necessary condition for amenability.

Recently, there has been a significant surge in research on the application of
prolinate spheroidal wave functions in multiple scientific disciplines, including
physics, optics, and signal processing. This study aims to provide a unified
approach to understanding PSWFs by focusing on their applications in quantum
mechanics and optics. We will explore the properties of the eigenvalues and
eigenfunctions of the PSWFs through a detailed analysis of the Schrödinger
equation, utilizing mathematical derivations and numerical computations.

We introduce a novel score function approach grounded in the principles of the Born-Oppenheimer potential energy surface, which is applicable to any crystal structure regardless of its atomic arrangement. This method is particularly advantageous as it does not rely on the presence of a periodic structure, allowing for the analysis of disordered systems. By utilizing this score function, we can obtain a simplified representation of the crystal structure, which is resistant to noise and can be used to identify key structural features. Furthermore, this score function can be used to generate a crystal structure with a specified atomic arrangement, which is a significant advantage for the study of materials science.

A Lagrangian approach is utilized to investigate the transport of water masses and associated properties in the ocean, with a focus on a specific region in the South China Sea. This study examines the movement of a virtual particle over a period of 100 days using drifter trajectory calculations based on high-resolution ocean current data. The resulting trajectory is then compared to a specific current jet in the region, and the evolution of water mass properties is analyzed through a 1D advection model. The research also explores the impact of varying initial conditions and datasets on the trajectory and property evolution of the virtual particle. The findings suggest that the virtual particle's trajectory is significantly influenced by its initial position and the quality of the ocean current data used, and the study highlights the challenges of using a Lagrangian approach in regions with complex ocean dynamics.

The scaling of thermodynamic properties in glass formation is a universal phenomenon that can be explained by the connection between entropy and structural characteristics. A key aspect of this explanation involves a quantity called configurational entropy density, which is derived from the random phase approximation. This paper demonstrates that a more precise calculation of this quantity, based on a more sophisticated theory of entropy, results in a more accurate description of thermodynamic scaling. This refined explanation is supported by numerical evidence from simulations of model glass formers, which show that a more accurate calculation of this quantity is achieved by considering the effects of short-range order in the system.

This paper explores the semi-discrete version of the modified Camassa-Holm equation through a nonlocal, semi-discrete hierarchy, which is derived from a Lax pair with a nonlocal, semi-discrete spectral problem.

In the context of the Pauli spin system, we examine how contextuality is influenced by the wave function, and we derive an equivalent expression for the Bell-Kochen-Specker inequality, taking into account the statistical properties of the quantum state.

The spin dynamics of compact binary systems, consisting of black holes or neutron stars, are influenced by gravitational interactions. This article delves into the spin dynamics of binary systems, focusing on the effects of spin-orbit and spin-spin couplings. It also explores the influence of spin precession on the orbital plane and symmetry of the emitted gravitational waves. Furthermore, an investigation is conducted into the spin precession effects on the binary's orbital parameters, specifically the orbital eccentricity and spin-orbit alignment angle.

In recent years, the YOLO (You Only Look Once) object detection approach has gained significant popularity due to its efficiency and effectiveness. Unlike two-stage region proposal models, YOLO can directly predict object bounding boxes and class probabilities from a single image, resulting in faster processing times. However, the original YOLO model's performance is limited by its reliance on a single neuron for each class, which can lead to suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a multi-branch network to predict bounding boxes and class probabilities. This approach, known as the multi-branch YOLO (MB-YOLO), involves the use of multiple branches, each with a unique set of convolutional filters, to generate a more accurate bounding box prediction. By incorporating a multi-branch structure, the model can capture a broader range of features and improve the overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed MB-YOLO model achieves superior performance compared to the original YOLO model on multiple datasets, including PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO.

The biographical connections dataset, known as CBDB, is a comprehensive resource for the Tang and Song Dynasty China, comprising over 200,000 biographical entries. A substantial portion of these entries contain extensive quotes, but the quoted information is often plagued by inaccuracies, such as unverified job titles and affiliations. This study presents a novel approach to identifying and categorizing job titles and affiliations from quoted text, thereby enabling the detection of inconsistencies and the differentiation between factual and spurious quotes. By leveraging the dataset, we aim to enhance the accuracy of quoted information and the overall quality of the CBDB resource.

Decision trees and their ensembles are widely utilized in supervised machine learning due to their interpretability and efficiency. However, the process of constructing decision trees is computationally intensive, particularly for large datasets. To address this issue, we introduce a novel algorithm that accelerates the decision tree construction process by leveraging a unique combination of data partitioning and tree-building techniques. Our approach involves splitting the dataset into smaller subsets, constructing individual trees for each subset, and then integrating the trees into a cohesive ensemble. To further optimize this process, we introduce a novel method for selecting the most suitable trees from the ensemble, which we demonstrate to outperform existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

The increasing adoption of machine learning in applications has led to a need for a comprehensive evaluation of models, considering factors such as accuracy, efficiency, and fairness. To address this challenge, we propose a holistic evaluation framework that assesses the performance of models in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and fairness. This framework is designed to be adaptable to various applications and can be used to compare different models. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply the framework to a range of models, including those based on deep learning and those utilizing approximate inference techniques. Our results show that the framework can effectively identify the most suitable model for a given application, taking into account multiple performance metrics.

This paper addresses the challenge of identifying and classifying newly emerging and rare subcategories in a continuous data stream. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach called RARE, which is a two-stage process. In the first stage, RARE utilizes a pre-trained, self-supervised model to extract relevant features from the input data. In the second stage, RARE applies a dynamic clustering algorithm to identify and adapt to newly emerging subcategories in real-time. Our approach is demonstrated through a case study using a dataset of tweets, showcasing its effectiveness in recognizing and classifying emerging and rare subcategories in a dynamic environment.

The application of coherent x-ray diffraction imaging has the potential to provide a significant breakthrough in the field of materials science by enabling the visualization of the internal structure of materials at the nanoscale. However, the effectiveness of this technique is hindered by the scattering of the x-ray beam within the sample, which can result in a distorted image. To overcome this limitation, a novel technique called ptychography has been developed to improve the imaging of highly scattering materials. In this study, we have successfully applied the ptychography technique to the in-situ imaging of the deformation of a single gold nanoparticle under the influence of a focused laser beam. By combining the ptychography technique with the analysis of the diffraction patterns, we have been able to reconstruct the phase of the x-ray beam and obtain a detailed image of the nanoparticle. Furthermore, we have used the phase information to calculate the strain within the nanoparticle and observed the formation of a dislocation loop under the influence of the laser beam. To validate our results, we have also performed finite element simulations of the deformation of the nanoparticle and found that the simulated strain distribution closely matches the experimental results obtained using ptychography. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the potential of the ptychography technique in the in-situ imaging of the deformation of highly scattering materials and provides valuable insights into the behavior of materials at the nanoscale.

Stochastic thermodynamics' scaled cumulant-generating functions have a notable gauge invariance, which is essential for accurately describing the statistical behavior of stochastic thermodynamic quantities. This work demonstrates that this property can be derived from the Kolmogorov forward equation, and consequently, it is possible to formulate it in terms of the probability current, which is a more intuitive approach. This formulation is then applied to a specific case, and the gauge invariance is shown to be consistent with previous research.

Reservoir computing is a type of complex system that can efficiently process information and has gained significant attention in recent years. Researchers have found that RCs composed of complex networks can achieve high performance, but the relationship between network structure and performance is still unclear. In this study, we investigate the performance of RCs composed of complex networks with different structures and find that their performance is closely related to the modularity and link density of the underlying network. We also discover that the memory capacity of RCs is influenced by the network's structural properties, and we find that a specific range of parameters can lead to optimal memory capacity. Our results provide new insights into the relationship between network structure and RC performance, and we hope that this study will contribute to the development of more efficient RCs.

A novel approach in quantum machine learning, quantum kernel methods, has been developed to enhance classical SVMs. This method employs quantum circuits to create a specific quantum kernel, which can be leveraged by a standard SVM algorithm. This paper proposes a hybrid SVM that utilizes quantum circuits to divide data into clusters and a classical SVM to classify within those clusters. This approach is demonstrated through simulations on real-world datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in classification tasks.

This text describes an approach to numerically approximate Newtonian potentials using an adapted form of Green's third identity, which incorporates a specially designed fundamental solution. This solution is a modified version of the Newtonian potential, which no longer has a singularity at the point of interest. By applying a weighted average of nearby function values, the method avoids the need for derivatives and can achieve second-order accuracy. This approach is particularly useful for solving boundary integral equations that arise in the solution of Poisson's equation.
